To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the citation‐based performance of a research field is correlated with its coauthorship pattern, and the correlation is a power law, and the exponent of this power law is 1.20; (2) the citations to a subfields research articles increase 2.20 times each time it doubles the number of coauthorship papers.
the citation‐based performance of a subfield's papers is strongly related to its coauthorship patterns.

the citation‐based performance of research articles in the natural sciences is strongly correlated to the coauthorship patterns of research articles, and the Matthew Effect is more pronounced in the coauthored research articles than in the single‐authored ones.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the power‐law scaling relationship between citation impact and coauthorship.
the relationship between citation‐ based performance and coauthorships in the natural sciences, and we have found a power‐law relationship.
the power‐law correlation between citation‐based research performance and the number of coauthors in research articles in the natural sciences.

the power‐law relationships between citation‐based impact and coauthorship pattern are different for single‐authord papers and papers written in coauthorship.

coauthored papers have an advantage in citation impact over single‐authored ones, but the advantage is not so great as to make it a universal rule.

the citation impact is a nonlinear function of the number of coauthors.
the Matthew Effect is stronger in the coauthored papers in the natural science.
the Matthew Effect is a strong force in the scientific world.

the citation‐based performance of papers is strongly related to their coauthorship patterns.
